catalog_quote: Primary stress is generally predictable based on the morphological structure of the item, falling on the first non-prefix syllable. Verbs ending in -earen represent an exception, with the penultimate syllable receiving primary stress, e.g. passearen /pə.ˈsia.ɾən/ ‘to happen’, opperearen /ɔ.pə.ˈɾia.ɾən/ ‘to operate’. Similarly, some borrowed lexemes show non-morphologically determined stress patterns, such as Perischkie /pə.ɾɪʃ.ˈki/ ‘pirozhki, fruit-filled pastries’ (< Rus. пирожки, Ukr. пиріжки) and Warenikje /və.ˈɾɛ.nɪ.kʲə/ ‘perogies’ (< Ukr./Rus. вареники); as do occasional items in the native Plautdietsch lexicon, such as (han) kefoojen /kə.ˈfəʊ.jən/ ‘to throw down forcefully’ and unjarenaunda /ˌʊ.ɲa.ɾəˈnaʊn.da/ ‘amongst, amidst, mixed’. new_statements.rule_in_words: Germanic stem-initial stress: primary stress falls on the first syllable of the stem (first non-prefix syllable), i.e. word-initial in unprefixed words. Exceptions: verbs in -earen (cf. German -ieren) stress the penult; some Slavic loans and a few native items have lexically fixed non-initial stress; separable vs inseparable prefixed verbs form stress minimal pairs (prefix-stressed vs stem-stressed).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as a rule; secondary stress is transcribed on the non-primary member in prefixed-verb minimal pairs (e.g. /ˌʊ.ɲa.ˈʃto.nən/ vs /ˈʊ.ɲa.ˌʃto.nən/) and in unjarenaunda /ˌʊ.ɲa.ɾəˈnaʊn.da/. Wiebe 1983 likewise marks secondary stress with ˌ but gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs in -earen (penultimate stress: passearen, opperearen); loans Perischkie (final), Warenikje (second syllable); native kefoojen, unjarenaunda; contrastive pairs unjastohnen, wadaholen (separable-prefix stress vs stem stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress in citation forms (IPA transcriptions of isolated lexical items); intonation treated separately at sentence level. Variety: Canadian Old Colony (Chortitza-descended) Plautdietsch, Blumenheim, Saskatchewan; Wiebe 1983 (Swift Current, Saskatchewan) independently states 'Stress usually falls on the first syllable unless otherwise noted' (p. 27 fn. 1).
new_statements.identity_note: Statement describes Canadian Old Colony (Chortitza/Reinländer-descended) Mennonite Plautdietsch as spoken in Blumenheim, Saskatchewan (JIPA Illustration speaker); Glottolog plau1238 covers all Plautdietsch varieties (no sub-dialect glottocodes). Wiebe 1983 (Swift Current, Saskatchewan) gives a concordant first-syllable default. The Glottolog bibliography for plau1238 also lists Volga German works (Johnson 1994, Keel 2004) which are not Plautdietsch and were ignored.

sources.note: p. 226 'Stress and intonation': primary stress generally predictable from morphology, on the first non-prefix syllable; verbs in -earen take penultimate stress; some loans (Perischkie, Warenikje) and a few native items have non-morphological stress; stress can be contrastive in separable vs inseparable prefix verbs (unjastohnen, wadaholen), with secondary stress marked on the other member.
